title: Eclipses
name: Eclipses
system: Sun · Earth · Moon — a near-perfect straight line
tagline: Same three objects as moon phases — but this time, almost perfectly in a line
summary: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes directly between the Sun and Earth, briefly blocking sunlight from a small part of Earth. A lunar eclipse happens when Earth passes directly between the Sun and Moon, casting Earth's shadow onto the Moon. Both need a near-perfect straight-line alignment, which is why eclipses are rare even though the Moon lines up roughly like this every single month — it's almost always just a little too high or too low.

whyItMatters: This is the clearest possible demonstration of why a 5.1° tilt matters: switch it off and this simulation would produce an eclipse every single month, which is not what actually happens. Real astronomy is full of small angles like this one quietly deciding whether a dramatic event happens or not.
didYouKnow: By pure coincidence, the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and also about 400 times farther away — which is why the Moon can almost exactly cover the Sun's disc during a total solar eclipse, something that isn't true for any other planet-moon pair we know of.
conditions: The Moon's 5.1° orbital tilt makes most months miss

compareReason: Both use exactly the same three-body geometry (Sun, Earth, Moon) — the only difference is how precise the alignment is. Comparing them directly is the fastest way to stop confusing 'New Moon' with 'solar eclipse.'
